description: A composite, six-row figure in which every row applies the same three-step segmentation pipeline to a different microstructure; the columns are headed "Image", "Overlay" and "Key structure". (a) is a grey micrograph with a fine dark globular/network phase; its Overlay adds a red segmentation mask and its Key structure panel is a white-on-black binary of that same network. (b) shows a coarser cellular network plus a few needle/rod-shaped precipitates, and its binary retains only the elongated needles, not the cell walls. (c) shows large elongated lenticular plates overlaid with a colour-per-region mask, whose binary reduces to a thin white boundary skeleton. (d) shows large grey grains cut by thick irregular dark bands (cracks), reproduced as white foreground in the binary. (e) and (f) — the only panels carrying printed labels, "C22000 (brass) twin grain" and "C21000 (brass) twin grain" — are pink/orange optical micrographs whose overlays colour whole grains and whose binaries mask straight, parallel-sided twin lamellae (one marked by a diagonal arrow). No axes, scale bars or numeric values are printed anywhere; panels (a)–(d) bear no visible letter labels in the supplied crops. Together the rows argue that one training-free model segments chemically, morphologically and defect-wise dissimilar microstructures across scales without annotations.

subfigures.description: Top row (no printed letter label in the crop; header reads 'Image  Overlay  Key structure'). Grayscale micrograph of a fine dark globular/network phase in a lighter matrix; the middle panel shows the raw image with a red segmentation overlay; the right panel is a black binary in which the segmented network appears as dense white speckle.

Second row. Grayscale micrograph of a coarser, cell/dendrite-like dark network with a few thin needle- or rod-shaped features; the overlay panel repeats the image with red masks, and the binary panel contains only the thin elongated needles as white lines on black (the cell walls are not foreground).

Third row. Grayscale micrograph dominated by large elongated lenticular/plate-shaped features separated by thin boundaries; the overlay panel tint-colours individual regions, and the binary panel shows a thin white boundary skeleton with black interiors.

Fourth row. Grayscale micrograph of large grains traversed by thick, irregular dark bands; the overlay panel colours grains, and the binary panel renders exactly those dark bands (cracks) as white foreground on black.

Fifth row, labelled '(e)  C22000 (brass)  twin grain'. Pink-toned optical micrograph with large equiaxed grains and straight parallel-sided twin lamellae; the overlay panel assigns a different colour to each grain and the binary panel masks the straight twin bands as white shapes with a diagonal arrow annotation.

Sixth row, labelled '(f)  C21000 (brass)  twin grain'. Orange/pink optical micrograph of a few large grains containing long, straight parallel-sided twin lamellae; the overlay colours the grains and the binary panel extracts the twin lamellae as elongated white strips.

observations.observation: Every row of the figure is a three-column comparison: the raw micrograph ('Image'), the same micrograph with a segmentation overlay ('Overlay'), and a black-background binary image showing the extracted object in white ('Key structure').
Panel (a) shows a fine, dense dark globular/network phase in a lighter matrix; its binary key-structure image reproduces that network as dense white speckle.
Panel (b) contains a coarser cell-like network plus a few thin needle/rod-shaped features, and only the elongated needles are retained as white foreground in its binary image.
Panel (c) is dominated by large elongated lenticular plates, and its binary output is a thin intergranular/boundary skeleton rather than filled grains.
Panel (d) shows large grains cut by thick irregular dark bands, and exactly those bands appear as white foreground in the binary image, i.e. they are the segmented target.
Panels (e) and (f) are optical micrographs of brass with straight parallel-sided twin lamellae inside large grains, and their binary panels extract those lamellae as elongated white strips.
No axes, coordinate labels, scale bars, magnification values or numeric annotations are printed in any panel of the supplied crops.
Only panels (e) and (f) carry printed labels ('(e) C22000 (brass) twin grain', '(f) C21000 (brass) twin grain'); the other rows have no visible panel letters in the supplied crops.
The caption identifies the six extracts as NBS-3 (γ' phase), NBS-3 (TCP phase), IN939-1 (melted pool boundary), IN939-2 (cracks), C22000 brass (twin grain) and C21000 brass (twin grain).

The caption states that in each row the first column is the raw image, the second column is a segmentation mask overlaid on the raw image, and the third column is a binary image highlighting different phases as foreground.

The citing text states that these are six additional micrographs (from ref. [50]) that are not provided with corresponding annotations, used to show the model's extensibility/generalizability in recognising microstructures of different scales and morphologies within a single micrograph.

The figure's overall claim is that one training-free segmentation approach transfers across chemically, morphologically and defect-wise different microstructures (γ' network, TCP needles, melt-pool boundaries, cracks, twin lamellae) without per-image annotation.
